claims.text: The name Telimektar is in Qenya. It is glossed as "Orion, literally Swordsman of Heaven" in the Qenya Lexicon, under the root TELE ("cover in"). The name is comprised of telimbo ("canopy, sky") + ektar ("swordsman").
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, "Qenyaqetsa: The Qenya Phonology and Lexicon", in Parma Eldalamberon XII (edited by Carl F. Hostetter, Christopher Gilson, Arden R. Smith, and Patrick H. Wynne), p. 90

claims.text: Telimektar is first mentioned in the Lost Tales in the story of the Chaining of Melko. There, he was "but just war-high" when he fought at his father's side against Melko in the war which ended with the captivity of the Enemy. In that story Telimektar had "a long sword girt about his waist by a silver girdle."
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Book of Lost Tales Part One, "IV. The Chaining of Melko", p. 101

claims.text: His next mention is during the Darkening of Valinor, where he was pursuing Melko along with the other Valar.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Book of Lost Tales Part One, "VI. The Theft of Melko and the Darkening of Valinor", p. 154

claims.text: However, Telimektar and Ingil had to remain in the sky, guarding ceaselessly until Melko's return in the Great End. There, Varda periodically gives him stars to replace the ones Melko destroys and to remind the world of the Valar's watch - and the constellation of Orion is afterwards seen as his image in the sky.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, Christopher Tolkien (ed.), The Book of Lost Tales Part Two, "VI. The History of Eriol or Ælfwine and the End of the Tales", outline 4, pp. 281-2

claims.text:
The Gnomish cognate of Telimektar is Telumaithor, with the earlier forms of the name being Telumaithron and Telumaithweg.
One of his names was Mordo. It is a Gnomish word adopted into Qenya, being derived from mavar ("shepherd") through Gnomish mord - its meaning being a poetic one for "man, warrior" or otherwise possibly derived from the "warlike qualities of the shepherds". A similar name was Taimordo (Taimondo being a corrupt form of the name), with Daimort (changed from Daimord) being its Gnomish cognate.
Another late name for the character was Telmaithron.
claims.cite: J.R.R. Tolkien, "I-Lam na-Ngoldathon: The Grammar and Lexicon of the Gnomish Tongue", in Parma Eldalamberon XI (edited by Christopher Gilson, Arden R. Smith, and Patrick H. Wynne), p. 70; J.R.R. Tolkien, "I-Lam na-Ngoldathon: The Grammar and Lexicon of the Gnomish Tongue", in Parma Eldalamberon XI (edited by Christopher Gilson, Arden R. Smith, and Patrick H. Wynne), p. 29; J.R.R. Tolkien, "Qenyaqetsa: The Qenya Phonology and Lexicon", in Parma Eldalamberon XII (edited by Carl F. Hostetter, Christopher Gilson, Arden R. Smith, and Patrick H. Wynne), p. 62; J.R.R. Tolkien, "Early Qenya and The Valmaric Script", in Parma Eldalamberon XIV (edited by Carl F. Hostetter, Christopher Gilson, Arden R. Smith, Patrick H. Wynne, and Bill Welden), "The Names of the Valar", p. 13

claims.text:
In one of the later outlines, which might have formed the basis for The Book of Lost Tales, Telimektar was said to have a son called Lúthien.
The idea of Telimektar and Ingil (known to Men in later ages as Orion and Sirius respectively) guarding against Melko's eventual return was ultimately abandoned. In its place, the idea of Eärendel keeping the watch on the Door of Night through which Melko/Morgoth was thrust at the end of the War of Wrath, was adopted instead.
Of the name Telimektar remained only the mention of Telumehtar as a name of Orion in the Appendices to The Lord of the Rings.
